newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romania's new private media thrive on election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romania's new private media thrive on election.

text.p: Romania's third post-communist election on Sunday shows the country has come a long way since the rallying call of "Let's take the radio and television!" rang across Bucharest during the 1989 revolution.
Viewers are bombarded nightly with speeches and debates by President Ion Iliescu and his 15 rivals for the presidency and thousands more seeking seats in parliament.
"Big brother" state media is gone.
The vacuum has been filled by scores of private radio and television stations, which are quickly winning over viewers from state broadcasters.
Surveys show that Romanian state television (TVR) still holds the lion's share with 80 percent of the audience. Public radio has more than 50 percent.
Private broadcasters, born after the 1992 general election, have been catching up fast, especially in big cities.
Nevertheless, it is in the remote rural areas, where state media still dominate, that the outcome of the November 3 elections will probably be decided.
Echoing the saying that whoever controls television holds power, the opposition accuses Iliescu's leftist ruling Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) of controlling the state media.

Iliescu's two main rivals, academic Emil Constantinescu of the Democratic Convention bloc, and Romania's first post-communist prime minister Petre Roman have complained about vicious attacks dealt at them through television clips.

"The PDSR has presented nasty videos with lies about me, because this is the type of campaign that Ion Iliescu and the PDSR are running -- a dirty and poisonous campaign," Roman told the private television channel Antena 1 last week.

A clip from Iliescu's campaign video shows Constantinescu's face fading away into that of exiled ex-king Michael, portraying the bearded academic as a closet monarchist -- a vote repellent in a country defined as a republic.
Opposition clips were equally negative. In a sign that taboos have fallen, one such spot juxtaposes Iliescu with late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu in rigid communist-era speechmaking.

Television is playing a novel role in the campaign -- to persuade Romanians to turn up at polling stations on Sunday. The lure -- lottery prizes equivalent to tens of thousands of dollars offered by both commercial and state channels.
The elections are also a vehicle for broadcasters to secure more freedom from regulatory bodies.
"We knew there would be lots of trouble during the campaign," said Mircea Baciu, one of the 11 members of the regulatory National Broadcasting Board (CNA).

Parties were alloted air time in keeping with their strength in parliament and Baciu said the CNA, modelled on France's broadcast watchdog, had warned state television that it had given too much air time to the PDSR and Iliescu.
Cracking the whip was also problem, and fines, up to five percent of a broadcaster's annual earnings, hard to levy.
"We can't really fine Romanian state television, for instance," Baciu said. "They're already mired in debts."

Besides the state media, 38 private local television stations and 78 radio broadcasters are covering the campaign. But the cable networks distributing most of them are banned from producing their own electoral programmes.
Cable television reaches two million households, or 7.5 million Romanians, according to unofficial statistics -- nearly half the number of voters.
Cable operators denounce the ban on programmes but the CNA says the restriction is meant to uphold quality.
"In Romania it's difficult to set limits. We must get closer to a fully-fledged democracy for people to understand that somebody should set the rules," said Baciu.
Commercial operators, unlike state channels, readily report blunders and events embarrassing for the ruling party.
Tele7 abc, a local private broadcaster, was the first to go public with the scandal earlier this month of a phony telephone survey conducted for the PDSR which was loaded against Iliescu's rivals.
Commercial television showed Iliescu jeered by protesters during campaign tours, his popularity eroded by seven years in power. No such news was broadcast on state channels.
Commercial broadcasters staged lively talk shows in sharp contrast to monotonous fare served up on public channels.

"There's no negative news coverage on state television. Commercial stations air critical reports about the campaign," said local journalist Mircea Toma. "There's been a big step forward from the previous polls in 1990 and 1992."
And just as the protesters ended an era by storming Romanian television in 1989, private broadcasters now say the media regulator should be scrapped after the elections.
"They (CNA) are like a leech. They do nothing but behave as though they created us," said Florin Bratescu, head of Antena 1, one of Romania's top three private television companies.
